results.title: Mazur–Orlicz Problem 79 has a negative answer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The claim of Problem 79 of the Scottish Book for the plane is false: there is a polynomial map $P$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ to itself with a polynomial two-sided inverse that is not of the form $x \mapsto Ax + c$ with $A$ an invertible real $2 \times 2$ matrix and $c \in \mathbb{R}^2$. results.title: Relatively free group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ is relatively free if it has a family $(x_i)_{i \in I}$ of elements that generates $G$ such that for every family $(y_i)_{i \in I}$ of elements of $G$ there is an endomorphism $\varphi$ of $G$ with $\varphi(x_i) = y_i$ for all $i \in I$.

results.title: Values of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a word $v$ in the free group on $n$ generators and a group $G$, the set of values of $v$ on $G$ is the set of elements $v(g_1, \dots, g_n)$ obtained by substituting elements $g_1, \dots, g_n \in G$ for the generators, that is, the set of images of $v$ under all homomorphisms from that free group to $G$.

results.title: Hall's verbal finiteness conjecture for relatively free groups (Kourovka 12.31)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for every relatively free group $G$, every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every word $v$ in the free group on $n$ generators, if $v$ takes only finitely many values on $G$, then the verbal subgroup $v(G)$ of $G$ generated by these values is finite.

results.title: Hall's conjecture fails for relatively free groups
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Hall's verbal finiteness conjecture for relatively free groups is false: there are a relatively free group $G$, a natural number $n$ and a word $v$ in the free group on $n$ generators such that $v$ takes only finitely many values on $G$ but the verbal subgroup $v(G)$ of $G$ generated by these values is infinite.

results.title: Normal series with infinite cyclic factors
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ has a normal series with infinite cyclic factors when there are a natural number $n$ and subgroups $1 = H_0 \le H_1 \le \cdots \le H_n = G$, each normal in $G$, such that every factor $H_{i+1}/H_i$ is infinite cyclic.

results.title: Outer automorphisms of groups with an infinite cyclic normal series (Kourovka 13.23)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The conjecture that every nontrivial group with a normal series with infinite cyclic factors has an automorphism that is not inner.

results.title: Only inner automorphisms despite an infinite cyclic normal series (Kourovka 13.23 refuted)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a nontrivial group $G$ with a normal series with infinite cyclic factors such that every automorphism of $G$ is inner. So the conjecture of Kourovka Problem 13.23 is false.

results.title: Multiplicatively independent bases

results.title: Cobham's theorem

results.title: Period of the base-$p$ expansion

results.title: Generating polynomial of the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, an element $\zeta \in R$ and a natural number $n$, the $n$-th first-kind Jacobi–Stirling generating polynomial is $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (X - i(i + \zeta))$ in $R[X]$.

results.title: First-kind Jacobi–Stirling numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, an element $\zeta \in R$ and natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling number $J(n,k;\zeta)$ is the coefficient of $X^k$ in the polynomial $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (X - i(i + \zeta))$ over $R$.

results.title: Initial row of the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every commutative ring $R$, every $\zeta \in R$ and every natural number $k$, the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling number $J(0,k;\zeta)$ equals $1$ if $k = 0$ and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: Recurrence for the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every commutative ring $R$, every $\zeta \in R$ and all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling numbers satisfy $J(n+1,k+1;\zeta) = J(n,k;\zeta) - n(n + \zeta)\,J(n,k+1;\zeta)$.

results.title: First-kind Jacobi–Stirling numbers vanish above the diagonal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every commutative ring $R$, every $\zeta \in R$ and all natural numbers $n < k$, the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling number $J(n,k;\zeta)$ equals $0$.

results.title: Diagonal of the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every commutative ring $R$, every $\zeta \in R$ and every natural number $n$, the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling number $J(n,n;\zeta)$ equals $1$.

results.title: Generating polynomial of the Legendre–Stirling numbers of the first kind
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, this is the polynomial $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \bigl(X - i(i+1)\bigr)$ with integer coefficients; for $n = 0$ it is the empty product $1$.

results.title: Legendre–Stirling numbers of the first kind
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the Legendre–Stirling number of the first kind $J(n, k; 1)$ is the coefficient of $x^k$ in the integer polynomial $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \bigl(x - i(i+1)\bigr)$, which is $1$ when $n = 0$. These are the Jacobi–Stirling numbers of the first kind $J(n, k; \zeta)$ at $\zeta = 1$.

results.title: Initial row of the Legendre–Stirling numbers of the first kind
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$, the Legendre–Stirling number of the first kind $J(0, k; 1)$ equals $1$ if $k = 0$ and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: Recurrence for the Legendre–Stirling numbers of the first kind
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the Legendre–Stirling numbers of the first kind satisfy $J(n + 1, k + 1; 1) = J(n, k; 1) - n(n + 1) \, J(n, k + 1; 1)$.

results.title: Legendre–Stirling numbers of the first kind vanish above the diagonal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n < k$, the Legendre–Stirling number of the first kind $J(n, k; 1)$ is $0$.

results.title: Diagonal Legendre–Stirling numbers of the first kind

results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the Legendre–Stirling number of the first kind $J(n, n; 1)$ equals $1$.

results.title: Instances of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is a triple $(n, E, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers (the arcs) and a natural number $K$ (the bound on the number of arcs).

results.title: Directed adjacency for MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers and natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the directed adjacency test of $E$ at $(u, v)$ returns true when the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$, and false otherwise.

results.title: Bounded reachability in a digraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $E$ be a finite list of ordered pairs of natural numbers, read as the arcs of a directed graph, and let $n$, $u$ and $v$ be natural numbers. Then $v$ is reachable from $u$ within $n$ steps along $E$ when there are natural numbers $w_0, w_1, \dots, w_k$ with $k \le n$, $w_0 = u$ and $w_k = v$ such that $(w_j, w_{j+1})$ occurs in $E$ for every $j < k$.

results.title: Well-formed MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(a, b)$ in $E$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and $a \ne b$; that is, $E$ lists distinct arcs without loops between vertices among $0, \dots, n - 1$.

results.title: Feasible MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is feasible when some sublist $F$ of $E$ (obtained by deleting entries of $E$) has at most $K$ entries and, for all vertices $u < n$ and $v < n$, $v$ is reachable from $u$ within $n$ steps along $E$ if and only if $v$ is reachable from $u$ within $n$ steps along $F$.

results.title: MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an instance of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

results.title: MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

results.summary: For all $f, g \in \mathbb{N}$ and every partner array $\mu$, the Hopcroft–Karp phase loop with fuel $f + g$ from $\mu$ returns the same partner array as the loop with fuel $g$ run from the result of the loop with fuel $f$ from $\mu$.

For every natural number $f$, running at most $f$ Hopcroft–Karp phases from $\mu$, stopping early when a phase finds no path, gives a valid partner array whose first free round, if defined, is at least $c + f$.

results.title: Closing a deficit of $f$ in $f$ Hopcroft–Karp phases

results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a valid partner array, $M$ a matching of the bipartite graph and $f \in \mathbb{N}$. If $M$ has at most $f$ more pairs than the matched pairs of $\mu$, then $M$ has at most as many pairs as the matched pairs of the partner array returned by the Hopcroft–Karp phase loop with fuel $f$ from $\mu$.

results.title: Selection sort
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Selection sort of a list $L$ over a linearly ordered type is defined recursively. If $L$ is empty, the result is the empty list at cost $0$. If $L$ has head $x$ and tail $L'$, minimum extraction from $L'$ with initial candidate $x$ yields a minimum $m$ and the list $r$ of remaining elements, and the result is $m$ followed by the selection sort of $r$. The cost is the sum of the costs of all these minimum extractions.

results.title: Cost of minimum extraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every element $c$ of a linearly ordered type and every list $L$ over it, minimum extraction from $L$ with initial candidate $c$ has cost exactly $|L|$, the length of $L$; that is, it performs exactly $|L|$ order comparisons.

results.title: Correctness of minimum extraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be an element of a linearly ordered type and $L$ a list over it, and let $(m, r)$ be the pair returned by minimum extraction from $L$ with initial candidate $c$. Then the list $m$ followed by $r$ is a permutation of the list $c$ followed by $L$, $m \le c$, and $m \le x$ for every element $x$ of $L$.

results.title: Correctness of selection sort
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the list returned by selection sort on $L$ is sorted in nondecreasing order (each entry is $\le$ every later entry) and is a permutation of $L$, so it preserves duplicate multiplicities.

results.title: Comparison count of selection sort
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, selection sort has cost exactly $n(n-1)/2$ in the model that charges one unit per order comparison; that is, it performs exactly $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.
